notes.title: Start here: an identity provider you can read end to end
notes.body:
dotnet-auth (NetAuth0) is a small Auth0-style identity provider in .NET: it logs users in and hands applications tokens. The `docs2/` folder is a course; this quest uses chapter 03, "OAuth2 & OIDC, Learned From This Code", which explains each idea with a link to the exact lines that implement it.

Read it in its five stages: the authorization request, PKCE, the token exchange, refresh token rotation, and signing keys. For each stage, open `OAuthService.cs` at the linked lines before reading on. Most of the security rules are one `if` statement each, so you can see exactly where a check happens and what would break without it.

The chapter also lists the repo's known weak spots; treat them as review practice, not as a recipe.

excerpts.quote: explain OAuth2/OIDC, PKCE, JWTs, refresh rotation, and key rotation **with code citations instead of definitions**.

readMore.why: The course overview and how the projects fit together.

notes.title: Core idea: a code is useless without the proof that goes with it
notes.body:
In the authorization code flow, the provider first gives the application a short-lived code, and the application then trades that code for tokens. The danger is that a code can be copied on the way (a log, a bad redirect). So the provider binds each code to several facts it checks again at the trade: which client asked, which redirect address was used, and a secret proof that only the original app knows.

While reading stages 1 to 3, make a list of everything stored on the code row and everything compared again at the exchange. Each comparison closes one specific attack, which the chapter's table names.

excerpts.quote: is a checklist — every line is a distinct attack it forecloses

readMore.why: The AuthorizationCode entity and its IsActive rule.

notes.title: Core idea: long-lived tokens need a way to notice theft
notes.body:
Access tokens here live for minutes, but refresh tokens live for days, so a stolen refresh token is a stolen session. The provider replaces each refresh token every time it is used and links the old and new tokens into a family. That link is what lets it react when an old copy shows up.

Signing keys have a related problem: when a key is replaced, tokens signed with the old one are still in circulation. Read stage 4 and stage 5 with one question in mind: what does the server keep around, and for how long, so that both honest clients and verifiers keep working?

excerpts.quote: A stolen one is a stolen session.

readMore.why: Signing, JWKS publication and the current key.

notes.title: Why there is no implicit flow
notes.body:
The key is right. The first check in `CreateAuthorizationCodeAsync` refuses anything but `response_type=code`. The old implicit flow returned tokens inside the URL fragment of the redirect, where browser history and Referer headers can leak them. The code flow returns only a short-lived code.

- PKCE is a code-flow feature; it is not why other types are refused.
- Speed plays no part in the reasoning.
- Discovery documents can list several response types; the restriction is a choice.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("Only response_type=code is supported.");
it returned tokens in URL fragments where they leak via browser history and Referer headers.

notes.title: Redirect URIs must match exactly
notes.body:
The key is right. `ValidateRedirectUri` accepts a request only if some registered URI satisfies `string.Equals(x.Uri, redirectUri, StringComparison.Ordinal)`. `/cb/extra` is a different string, so it throws "redirect_uri is not registered."

- Prefix matching is the classic OAuth hole the chapter warns about.
- Matching the host is not enough; the whole string is compared.
- The rule is the same for every client type.

excerpts.quote: string.Equals(x.Uri, redirectUri, StringComparison.Ordinal)
This single check is what stops an attacker from receiving your authorization code

notes.title: PKCE ties the code to a secret the app never sent
notes.body:
The key is right. At authorize time the app sends only `code_challenge = SHA256(verifier)`, stored on the code row. At exchange time it must present the raw verifier; the server hashes it and compares with `FixedTimeEquals`. An attacker with the code but not the verifier fails "PKCE verification failed."

- Codes are not bound to IP addresses.
- Codes are random strings, not encrypted with a client secret; a SPA has no secret.
- The token endpoint never asks for the user's password.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("PKCE verification failed.");
still can't redeem it without the verifier, which never left the legitimate client.

notes.title: The plain method removes the hash
notes.body:
The key is right. In the exchange switch, `"plain" => request.CodeVerifier`: the expected challenge is the verifier itself. So the value sent at authorize time is the same secret needed at exchange time, and anyone who saw the first request can redeem the code.

- The redirect comparison runs for every method.
- Code lifetime is fixed at 5 minutes whatever the method.
- `ValidatePkce` still requires a challenge when the client requires PKCE.

excerpts.quote: "plain" => request.CodeVerifier,
with `plain`, stealing the challenge *is* stealing the verifier.

notes.title: Single-use holds only one request at a time
notes.body:
The key is right. Both requests load the row while `ConsumedAt` is still null, so both pass `IsActive`. `code.Consume(...)` only changes memory and is saved later. The `AuthorizationCode` mapping has a unique index on `CodeHash` but no concurrency token, so the second save does not fail.

- No 409 can come from EF without a concurrency token.
- The code takes no row lock.
- ConsumedAt is set after validation, near the end.

excerpts.quote: code.Consume(clock.UtcNow);
so two requests that load the same unconsumed code at the same moment both pass line 123 and both get tokens.

notes.title: The second redirect check binds code and redirect
notes.body:
The key is right. The code row stores the redirect URI used at authorize time, and the exchange compares it with the one presented now (`redirect_uri mismatch.`). That proves the party redeeming the code saw the same redirect the code was issued for, which blocks mix-up attacks.

- Authorize did validate it, exactly; this is a second, different check.
- Tokens are returned in the HTTP response to the caller, not posted to the URI.
- Client secrets are checked separately, earlier in the exchange.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("redirect_uri mismatch.");
it proves the exchanger saw the same redirect the code was issued for

notes.title: A dead token showing up revokes the whole family
notes.body:
The key is right. RT1 has `ReplacedById` set, so `IsActive` is false. The service calls `RevokeFamilyForReuseAsync`, which loads every token with the same `FamilyId`, calls `MarkReuse` on each (reuse time and revoked time), and writes `refresh_token.reuse_detected`.

- The server cannot tell thief from victim, so it does not keep RT2 alive.
- An inactive token is never accepted again.
- No new child is minted on reuse; the request fails.

excerpts.quote: item.MarkReuse(clock.UtcNow);
RT1,RT2,RT3 all marked reused+revoked

notes.title: Expiry is checked before reuse
notes.body:
The key is right. The first test after loading is `if (existing.ExpiresAt <= clock.UtcNow)`: the token is revoked, saved, and the call fails with "Refresh token expired." The reuse check comes after, so it never runs for an expired token.

- No family revocation or reuse audit happens on this path.
- Expiry is checked; it is the very first check.
- Users are blocked only by an admin action, not by this method.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("Refresh token expired.");
an *expired* token is revoked quietly without family revocation.

notes.title: The refresh path forgets the blocked flag
notes.body:
The key is right. Lines 205-207 load the `User` for the token, but nothing reads `user.IsBlocked` before new tokens are issued. The authorize path checks it (`"User is blocked."`, lines 36-40), and so does login, so the refresh path is the odd one out.

- That error message exists only on authorize and login.
- Nothing revokes the family for a blocked user here.
- The new access token carries the usual claims.

excerpts.quote: await db.Users.SingleAsync(x => x.Id == existing.UserId, cancellationToken);
Lines 205-207 load the `User` but never look at `IsBlocked`

notes.title: Retired keys stay published for a week
notes.body:
The key is right. `GetJwksAsync` returns keys where `RetiredAt == null || RetiredAt > clock.UtcNow.AddDays(-7)`. Rotation retires the old key; it is still in the JWKS, and the token's `kid` header selects it, so the signature verifies.

- No restart is needed for rotation.
- JwtBearer always validates the signature.
- Rotation creates a fresh RSA-2048 key; it is not derived from the old one.

excerpts.quote: .Where(x => x.RetiredAt == null || x.RetiredAt > clock.UtcNow.AddDays(-7))
A verifier that fetched JWKS and found only the new `kid` would reject *valid* tokens.

notes.title: Asymmetric signing keeps the signing key in one place
notes.body:
The key is right. HS256 uses one shared secret for signing and verifying, so every API that verifies tokens could also create them. With RS256 the provider signs with a private key and publishes only the public part, so resource servers can verify but not forge.

- HS256 tokens can carry a `kid` too; rotation is not the issue.
- Size and cost are not the chapter's argument.
- JwtBearer supports HS256; the choice is about trust.

excerpts.quote: HS256 is symmetric — every verifier holds the *signing* key, so any resource server could forge tokens.

notes.title: Without an audience check, any client's token fits
notes.body:
The key is right. The JwtBearer options set `ValidateIssuer = true` but `ValidateAudience = false`, so the API never asks which application the token was minted for. If a token for some other client carries the right permission claims, the admin API accepts it.

- Lifetime is still validated; expired tokens fail.
- Issuer is validated, so foreign issuers fail.
- Signature validation stays on, so unsigned tokens fail.

excerpts.quote: ValidateAudience = false,
so a token minted for any client works against the admin API if it carries the right permission claims.

notes.title: Codes are stored as hashes with a short life
notes.body:
The key is right. The service mints `secrets.UrlSafe(32)` and stores `secrets.Sha256Base64Url(code)` with an expiry of `clock.UtcNow.AddMinutes(5)`. `AuthorizationCode.IsActive` requires `ConsumedAt is null && ExpiresAt > now`, so a code works once and only briefly.

- The plain code is never stored, only its hash.
- BCrypt is used for passwords and client secrets, which can be low-entropy; a 32-byte random code needs only a fast hash.
- Codes are random strings, not JWTs.

excerpts.quote: clock.UtcNow.AddMinutes(5)
public bool IsActive(DateTimeOffset now) => ConsumedAt is null && ExpiresAt > now;
